# merge

Merge queue: worktree branches merged into the session they were built on, or into the main checkout.

- **Runs in:** the harness process
- **Source:** [lisp/modules/harness-merge.el](../../lisp/modules/harness-merge.el)
- **Loaded:** when enabled (see `harness-enable-modules`)
- **Requires:** [session](session.md), [agent](agent.md)
- **Brings along:** [ui-merge](ui-merge.md) (its UI), [tools](tools.md) (its file requires it)

## About

A session working in a git worktree asks for its branch to be merged
with `merge/enqueue`, naming the *target*: the session whose working
directory the branch merges into, or, for a task's branch, the main
checkout itself (a directory).  One queue per target, served one
merge at a time: the head of the queue takes the target's lock when
that session is idle, or when its running turn reaches a step
boundary (the `agent/step` and `agent/before-turn` filters hold it
until the lock is free again).  A main checkout has no session to
hold: its merges start as soon as the lock is free.

Targets nest.  A session may itself work in a worktree -- a task's
session does -- and start sub-agents in worktrees of their own, each
of which asks for a merge into it; its own branch, in turn, asks for
a merge into the main checkout.  Both levels are the same queue, the
same conflict resolution and the same events.  Order is built in:
a session's branch may be queued upward, but it waits there while
the merges into its own working directory are still queued, merging
or in conflict, so work reaches the main checkout in the order it
was built.  A session with such merges pending may not hand in
either (`merge/pending`, which the hand_in tool consults).

A merge is a transaction: the parent's checkout only ever moves by
a fast-forward to a finished commit, never through a merge in
progress.  `git merge-tree --write-tree` merges the child's branch
into the parent's HEAD without touching any working tree or index;
a clean result becomes ONE commit (`git commit-tree`), whose only
parent is the parent's HEAD, and `git merge --ff-only` moves the
parent's checkout onto it.  So a branch lands as a single readable
commit -- a pull request's worth of work -- rather than carrying
every small commit its agent made into the target's history: the
child's commits are not ancestors of the target afterwards.  The
commit's subject is the child session's name and its body lists the
commits the branch brings and their diffstat
(`harness-merge--message`), which is what makes the history legible
with so many tasks merging.

A branch whose work is already in the target -- merged before, or
the same change committed here -- leaves nothing to commit: a merge
whose tree equals the target's own tree is done with, without a
commit (`harness-merge--run-git-merge`).  The `git merge-base
--is-ancestor' fast path catches a branch that is in history; the
tree comparison catches one that was squashed in.

A task that carries on after it was merged -- sent back to work, or
prompted again -- needs the tip it last merged as the base of its
next merge.  git cannot find it (a squash commit leaves the branch's
commits out of the target's history), so the merge writes it to
`refs/harness/merged/BRANCH` and passes it to `git merge-tree
--merge-base' (`harness-merge--merge-base`): without it, the merge
would replay the work the target already holds and conflict with its
own squash commit.  A conflict still goes the way below -- the child
merges the target's HEAD into its branch and resolves there -- and
the re-queued branch then merges cleanly.

The fast-forward is all or nothing: git refuses it, changing
nothing, when it would overwrite uncommitted or untracked work in
the parent's checkout, or when a merge or rebase is in progress
there.  When the parent's HEAD moved meanwhile, the merge is
computed again.  So work someone left in the parent's checkout is
never lost, and a harness that stops mid-merge leaves the checkout
as it was.

A conflict never reaches the target's checkout.  The lock goes at
once and the target's HEAD has to be merged into the child's branch,
in the child's worktree, the conflicts resolved there and committed;
the `merge_done` tool then queues the branch again.  A safety timer
gives up on a conflict nobody resolves.

Who resolves them is `harness-merge-conflict-resolver`.  By default
the harness starts a fresh session for it (a `subagent` child of the
child session, in the child's worktree) with only the conflict to go
on: a child that finished long ago and waited in a queue has a cold
prompt cache and a long context, so waking it up to resolve a few
files would pay for its whole history again.  When that session's
turn ends without `merge_done` having queued the branch again, the
merge fails.  It runs on the child's model capped at the medium tier
of its provider, thinking no harder than that tier
(`harness-merge-resolver-model`): a few conflicting files need no
expensive model.  With `child`, the child session itself is steered
to resolve them, as before.

The fresh session shows in the child's transcript as a spawn_agent
call, as a sub-agent the child started would: the call once its turn
starts, its result -- the resolver's last reply, an error unless
merge_done queued the branch again -- when it stops.  The merge
queue made that call, not the child's model, and both nodes say so
(`harness-outside-node-p`): they never reach the child's model, so
its conversation is the same as without them.

The harness locks the worktrees it makes so that `git worktree
prune' keeps them (see harness-worktree.el).  Once a child's branch
is merged its work is safe on the parent's branch, so the lock goes
(`worktree/unlock`, which lifts only the harness's own locks) and the
worktree can be pruned again.  A merge that fails, is aborted or is
cancelled leaves the lock on.

Everything runs asynchronously through `harness-run-command`.

## Provides

### Methods

- `merge/cancel` (child-id) — Remove CHILD-ID from its merge queue.
- `merge/enqueue` (child-id target &rest opts) — Queue CHILD-ID's worktree branch for a merge into TARGET.
- `merge/pending` (session-id) — Return the merges SESSION-ID waits for, as `merge/queue` items.
- `merge/queue` (target) — Return the merge queue of TARGET: a session id, or a main checkout's directory.
- `merge/status` (child-id) — Return the merge status of CHILD-ID (queued, merging, conflict) or nil.
- `merge/view` (target) — Return the merge queue of TARGET as a session's chat shows it.

### Tools

- `merge_done` — Call after resolving the merge conflicts the merge queue handed to you: verifies that your worktree merged the parent's commit and committed the result, then queues your branch to merge again.

### Events

- `merge/conflict` — (CHILD-ID TARGET FILES) when a merge would conflict; they are resolved in the child's worktree.
- `merge/finished` — (CHILD-ID TARGET STATUS) merged, failed, aborted or cancelled.
- `merge/queued` — (CHILD-ID TARGET POSITION) after a merge was requested, TARGET naming the queue: the session the branch merges into, or a main checkout's directory.
- `merge/resolver` — (CHILD-ID TARGET RESOLVER-ID) when a fresh session starts resolving a merge's conflicts.
- `merge/started` — (CHILD-ID TARGET) when a merge takes its target's lock.

### Options

- `harness-merge-conflict-resolver` — Who resolves the conflicts of a merge the merge queue cannot make.
- `harness-merge-resolver-model` — Model of the fresh session that resolves merge conflicts.
